prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, opening a new regime of precision in the measurement of time

statement.case_for: The optical lattice clock is a measurement advance with numbers that can be checked. Katori's magic-wavelength proposal removes the light shift from the clock transition while thousands of atoms are trapped in the Lamb-Dicke regime, and Ye's strontium clocks turned that into fractional systematic uncertainties near 1e-18 and stability that averages down far faster than any single-ion clock. Many independent laboratories (RIKEN/Tokyo, JILA, SYRTE, PTB, NIST and others) now compare clocks at this level, which is the strongest form of reproducibility I know. The payoff is already visible: millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, bounds on drifts of fundamental constants, dark-matter searches, relativistic geodesy and the ongoing road map to a redefinition of the second. As an experimentalist I value that a new technique opened a new precision regime and enabled others to do physics they could not do before. The two-name attribution is also unusually clean: concept and first realization on one side, record performance on the other.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is overlap with earlier prizes: the 2005 prize on laser-based precision spectroscopy and the frequency comb (Ye was a close collaborator of Hall), and the 2012 prize on controlling single quantum systems including ion clocks. A sceptic can say this is a very successful incremental step on honoured foundations, and that the lattice clock is a technology whose largest scientific payoff, a redefined second and new physics tests, has not yet fully arrived. There is also the question of Lemonde, Derevianko, Ludlow, Takamoto and the Yb and Sr groups at SYRTE, PTB and NIST, whose contributions to the accuracy record are real and not in the credited names. Finally, the prize would credit only two people, one of whom already has a Nobel-adjacent association with the comb story, so the committee must be sure the lattice clock stands as a distinct achievement.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B013 first, arguing that the lattice clock turns a conceptual idea (magic wavelength) into measurable physics at 1e-18 and that it is a natural continuation after the comb and ion-clock prizes, with contributions by Lemonde, Derevianko and Ludlow being secondary.
responses.response: I agree on the central point and on the cleanness of the two-name attribution. I would qualify the word secondary. Lemonde's early lattice-clock work and the Sr and Yb comparisons at SYRTE, PTB and NIST are what made the 1e-18 claim credible, because an accuracy figure only counts once independent clocks agree. That is a reason to word the citation around the invention and realization of the technique rather than around a single accuracy record, and I do not think it is a reason to add names. Where we may differ is B050: I rank it below the clock because its payoff in answering open Hubbard questions is still partial, whereas the clock's measured performance is already delivered.

responses.point: Pearce ranks the IceCube neutrino discovery first as a detector-driven opening of a new observational window, and he places the lattice clock third while stating that atomic physics is outside his expertise and that he relies on atomic colleagues for credit and overlap questions.
responses.response: I share the instrument-driven criterion, and that is why I rank the clock first: a new measurement technique with quantifiable, repeatedly confirmed performance. On IceCube I accept the 2013 diffuse flux as firmly established, but I would press on maturity. The source picture rests on a handful of modest-significance associations, and the credit among Halzen, Karle, Spiering and the AMANDA and Baikal predecessors is not settled in the supplied names. The clock has no comparable ambiguity in the discovery itself. On the overlap with earlier prizes that Pearce raises, I would say the 2005 prize rewarded the comb as a ruler and the 2012 prize rewarded control of single ions, while the lattice clock rests on a different idea, many-atom interrogation with a cancelled light shift, so I do not see it as duplicating either.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the Event Horizon Telescope first and the lattice clock second, calling it a clean, nature-facing achievement, while noting that Ye's earlier 2005 prize may count against it for some members and that he prefers directly observed results over unconfirmed theory.
responses.response: I agree that overlap is the main objection, but Ye did not share the 2005 prize. It went to Hall and Hänsch, and Ye was a collaborator in the comb work, so the claim that a laureate is being honoured twice does not apply. Even so, the substantive question of distinctness remains and I take it seriously. I would be uneasy placing B016 above the clock. The imaging is spectacular, but a credit problem arises because the result belongs to a collaboration of hundreds, and the two- or three-name selection among Falcke, Doeleman and Zensus is, as you say yourself, contestable. For the clock, the discoverers are identifiable and the central quantity, fractional uncertainty, can be compared across laboratories.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks twisted bilayer graphene first as a robust, widely reproduced discovery where experiment overturned expectation and continuum theory has been tested, and he ranks the lattice clock seventh, deferring to atomic physicists on priority.
responses.response: The moiré case has real strength, and the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction followed by the 2018 experiments is the pattern I also value. My reservation is timing and attribution rather than merit. The pairing mechanism is not understood, twist-angle disorder still affects sample-to-sample reproducibility, and the first author of the discovery paper, Yuan Cao, cannot be credited, so the experimental side is a judgment call among several groups. Since you defer to atomic physicists on the clock, I can state its status directly: the performance has been reproduced by independent groups at the 1e-18 level and clock comparisons are routine, which is a more mature evidence base than B046 currently has. If the committee prefers a condensed matter prize I would not oppose B046 on science, but I would ask for a later year.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize, or sees it as incremental.
Whether Lemonde, Derevianko and the Sr and Yb groups at SYRTE, PTB and NIST warrant mention in the citation, and I have not independently verified early priority dates.
Whether a redefinition of the second, now under discussion, will be completed soon enough to strengthen the case, or whether the committee prefers to wait for it.
How strongly to weigh B037 and B009 against B013 if colleagues regard the squeezed-light or NV sensing cases as having cleaner attribution.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B013: I have no Lund, mentor or company connection to Katori or Ye. I note two weaker links. My alternatives B009 and B037 are measurement-oriented and sit near my own quantum optics and sensing interests, and my role in the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology overlaps institutionally with Johansson's home at Chalmers, which matters for B054 and not for my preferred option.
